title: Charles House
annotation_credit: Notes and colour highlights: Adam Hingston, 2026.
note: I'm interested in how the openings link these rooms without making them feel like one large space. There's a view through to the garden, but each room still has an edge of its own. It's a useful way to think about sharing a home while finding a little space for yourself.

title: Mahogany House
annotation_credit: Notes and colour highlights: Adam Hingston, 2026.
note: The table in the courtyard gives the spaces around it somewhere to come together. I like that the outdoor area feels connected to the rooms on either side, with space to sit as well as move through. It makes me think about what a shared terrace could offer two households.

title: 3 Generation House
architect: BETA office for architecture and the city
annotation_credit: Notes and colour highlights: Adam Hingston, 2026.
note: The stair is right beside the kitchen and dining table, so moving between levels is part of the life of the home. For my stacked apartments, the question is how to make that family connection feel easy while keeping each household's own way in.

title: Veil + Co. House
annotation_credit: Notes and colour highlights: Adam Hingston, 2026.
note: This covered route gives the walk between spaces a sense of shelter. The openings along it let someone step inside or keep moving. I'm interested in how a gallery could offer that same feeling of arriving home, with a clear route past the places where people might stop.

title: La Borda
annotation_credit: Notes and colour highlights: Adam Hingston, 2026.
note: The separate doors are easy to pick out, even though they face the same courtyard. Plants and small things along the galleries suggest ways people can make the edge of a home their own. I keep coming back to how these spaces can leave room to pause without taking over the shared route.

title: Marmalade Lane
annotation_credit: Notes and colour highlights: Adam Hingston, 2026.
note: The lane feels like more than a way to get from one door to another. The low walls, planting and places to sit give it an everyday domestic scale. I'm interested in how that feeling might carry into an apartment building, where a shared walkway can still feel close to home.
